overview.description: KnÃ¼ffeln (also known as KnÃ¼ffeler) is a traditional trick-taking game from North Germany (Oldenburg and Friesland) that belongs to the ancient KarnÃ¶ffel family. It is distinct for its complex 'Elected Suit' ranking, legal partnership communication, and the use of the 'KarnÃ¶ffel' (Unter) as the master card. It is one of the oldest game formats still played in Europe.

history.origins: Derived directly from the 15th-century KarnÃ¶ffel, it preserved the unique medieval ranking systems that most other card games lost. KnÃ¼ffeln specifically became associated with the farming communities of Oldenburg.
timeline: 1400s: KarnÃ¶ffel group games appear across Germany.
1800s: KnÃ¼ffeln becomes a standardized regional variant in Friesland.
1990s: Efforts by regional clubs to preserve the game through tournaments.
Present: Played competitively in the Oldenburg region of Germany.
history.evolution: The game retains the 'No Trump' terminology; instead, it uses an 'Elected Suit' with partial beaters (e.g., cards that only beat Kings).
history.cultural: Historically seen as a game of 'common folk' due to its ability for low cards (like the 6 or 7) to defeat royalty.

setup.deck: 48 cards. Use two sets of 24 cards or remove Aces from 52. Standard ranks 2-10, Jack, Queen, King.
setup.dealing: Each player receives 9 cards (dealt 3-3-3). One card is turned up to determine the elected suit.

rules.objective: Partnerships aim to win at least five of the nine tricks in each deal; the first team to reach five tricks wins the hand.
rules.gameplay:
1. Standard lead-based play.
2. **No Follow Suit**: Players are NOT required to follow suit or rank. They can play any card at any time.
3. **Partnership Talk**: Partners can freely show cards and discuss strategy during the round.
keyRules: No follow-suit requirement; players may play any card at any time.
Elected suit (determined by turned card) has special ranking: matadors, beaters, then plain cards.
Partners may openly communicate and bluff; first team to win five of nine tricks wins the hand.

strategy.basic: Identify the Master cards (Unter, 6, 2) in your team immediately. Coordinate with your partner so that you don't 'clash' your high cards on the same trick.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Seven' Trap: Use your Seven (The Devil) only when you are in the lead. It is your only 'free' trick-winner. If you hold it until the end, it will likely be beaten by a plain card.
strategy.advanced: Managing the Plain Kings: Since the 3, 4, and 5 of trumps can only beat Kings/Obers, use them to 'kill' the opponents' high plain-suit cards so your partner's plain Kings become the master of their own suit.
tips: Because there is no obligation to follow suit, you can 'hide' your KarnÃ¶ffel until the very last trick of a 5-trick run.
Always communicate! If you have the 4-beater, tell your partner so they don't waste their Kaiser.

difficulty.easy: Fails to communicate with partner; leads 'The Devil' incorrectly; follows suit unnecessarily.
difficulty.hard: Expert at partner-signaling; perfectly exploits the 'No Follow Suit' rule to bait out opponents' Master cards.

engine.deckDescription: A 48-card pack formed by removing the Aces from a standard 52-card French deck. Four suits (Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs, Spades), each with twelve ranks: 2 through 10, Jack, Queen, and King. Used for Knüffeln and other Karnöffel-family games.
engine.suitDescription: Four traditional French suits: Hearts (Cœur), Diamonds (Carreau), Clubs (Trèfle), and Spades (Pique), each represented with standard French card iconography and distinct color coding for easy identification.
engine.rankDescription: Twelve ranks per suit: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, Jack, Queen, and King. Aces are removed; the Unter (Jack of chosen suit) and certain low cards have special powers in the elected-suit hierarchy.
